title: Pioneers, Guideposts and the Logic of Guidance Cues

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Why does an axon often navigate a long route as a sequence of legs?
cards.back: A growth cone reads only nearby information. At each choice point, a new cue or a changed response to an existing cue selects the next leg.
cards.quote: A growth cone reads only what is within its reach. So a long route is usually built as a chain of legs.

cards.front: The moving tip of a growing axon is the {{c1::growth cone}}.
cards.back: It contains actin and filopodia, backed by microtubules from the axon shaft.
cards.quote: The growth cone is the moving tip of a growing axon: a fan of actin with fingers called filopodia, backed by microtubules from the axon shaft.
cards.section: What a growth cone can read

cards.front: Which two properties define the four classes of axon guidance cue?
cards.back: Contact versus action at a distance, and attraction versus repulsion: contact attraction, contact repulsion, long-range attraction and long-range repulsion.
cards.quote: And does it draw the growth cone in or push it away?
cards.section: What a growth cone can read

cards.front: Give one matrix example and one axon-surface example of contact attraction for growth cones.
cards.back: Laminin in the extracellular matrix; L1 on other axons.
cards.quote: Is the cue fixed to a cell or to the matrix between cells, so that it acts on contact,
cards.section: What a growth cone can read

cards.front: Which cell-surface cue provides an example of contact repulsion for growth cones?
cards.back: Ephrins: growth cones with the matching Eph receptor collapse and retreat on contact.
cards.quote: And does it draw the growth cone in or push it away?
cards.section: What a growth cone can read

cards.front: Which cue attracts commissural axons across a gel in culture, illustrating long-range attraction?
cards.back: Netrin-1. Its ability to act across a gel does not establish its range in an embryo.
cards.quote: Netrin-1 was long taught as the classic long-range attractant in the embryo too, but in mice much of its effect turns out to be local,
cards.section: What a growth cone can read

cards.front: Which secreted cue repels growth cones across a collagen gel, illustrating long-range repulsion?
cards.back: Sema3A, a secreted semaphorin.
cards.quote: And does it draw the growth cone in or push it away?
cards.section: What a growth cone can read

cards.front: A growth cone retreats from a diffusible cue before touching the cells releasing it. How would you classify this response, and why?
cards.back: Long-range repulsion: the cue acts at a distance and pushes the growth cone away.
cards.quote: or is it released and spread through the tissue, so that it acts at a distance?
cards.section: What a growth cone can read

cards.front: Why does an axon turning toward a pipette releasing an attractant demonstrate more than an increase in growth rate?
cards.back: The growth cone changes direction up the gradient. This is chemotropism; faster extension alone would not demonstrate steering.
cards.quote: The turn was more than faster growth, which is what makes it chemotropism (they called it chemotaxis): steering up a gradient.
cards.section: What a growth cone can read

cards.front: A cue steers growth cones near a releasing pipette. Is that enough to conclude that one embryonic source can guide an entire long axon route?
cards.back: No. The pipette establishes steering near a steep gradient. The local-reading rule and loss of detectable differences with distance mean that reach and later choice points remain untested.
cards.quote: Close to a pipette tip the gradient is steep, so the assay shows what a growth cone can read near a source,
cards.section: What a growth cone can read

cards.front: The first axons through a territory are called {{c1::pioneers}}.
cards.back: They have no earlier axons to follow through that territory.
cards.quote: The first axons through a territory are pioneers.

cards.front: How do a guidepost cell and an intermediate target each mark a choice point for an axon?
cards.back: A guidepost is a cell touched at a turn. An intermediate target is a place the axon reaches and then leaves for its next leg.
cards.quote: intermediate targets, places an axon grows to and then leaves for its next leg, such as the ventral midline that commissural axons cross.

cards.front: Why can a secreted cue become unreadable to a growth cone far from its source?
cards.back: As the cue spreads and thins, the concentration difference between the two sides of the growth cone can fall below noise.
cards.quote: A secreted cue thins as it spreads, and far enough away the difference across a growth cone is lost in noise.

cards.front: Two identical attractant sources lie on opposite sides of a growth cone at equal distances in uniform tissue. What happens to their directional pulls, and why?
cards.back: The pulls can cancel: neither source provides a stronger directional influence at that symmetric location.
cards.quote: and between two equal sources the pulls can cancel.

cards.front: A follower axon travels around a long curve along a pioneer without meeting a separate guidepost cell. Does that contradict guidance by local readings? Explain.
cards.back: No. The rule requires information within reach, not a new cell at every turn. A continuous contact pathway can be long and curved, so local contact can support the whole curve.
cards.quote: A contact pathway, such as a laminin track or a pioneer axon, can be long and curved,

cards.front: In the grasshopper leg, destroying Cx1 before Ti1 arrives produces abnormal routes. What does this establish, and what remains unknown?
cards.back: Cx1 is needed for the normal turn in this preparation. The result does not identify whether Cx1 supplies adhesion or a signal.
cards.quote: It does not say what Cx1 provides, whether adhesion or a signal.

cards.front: After focused-light destruction of a candidate guidepost, axons misroute. Design a nearby-light control and state the alternative explanation it tests.
cards.back: Aim light beside the guidepost without destroying it, then score the route. Mostly normal routes would argue against nearby light damage alone explaining the misrouting.
cards.quote: Touching is not needing: the growth cones might touch Cx1 and turn there for some other reason.

cards.front: An axon leaving its bundle undergoes {{c1::defasciculation}}.
cards.back: Bundled growth is fasciculation.
cards.quote: When axons grow bundled together they are fasciculated; when one leaves its bundle it defasciculates.

cards.front: How does the labeled pathway hypothesis explain a follower growth cone choosing one axon bundle among several?
cards.back: Bundles carry surface labels; a growth cone has receptors for some labels, allowing selective recognition rather than indiscriminate following.
cards.quote: This led to the labeled pathway hypothesis: each bundle carries surface labels, and each growth cone has receptors for some of them.

cards.front: Grasshopper G axons travel normally after A neurons are killed, but wander after P neurons are killed despite other bundles being within reach. What does this comparison show?
cards.back: G depends on something particular to P axons, rather than merely needing any nearby bundle or the A/P bundle as a whole.
cards.quote: Other bundles were within reach of G's filopodia, yet G did not take one, and losing the A axons from the same bundle did not matter.

cards.front: How did fly adhesion findings revise the idea that each axon bundle has a unique surface label?
cards.back: They identified molecules controlling bundling rather than a unique label for every bundle; the amount of adhesion also influences pathway choice.
cards.quote: It found adhesion molecules that control which axons bundle together, rather than a unique label for each bundle, which revised the hypothesis.

cards.front: Fasciclin II binds {{c1::Fasciclin II}} on a neighbouring axon.
cards.back: This is homophilic adhesion.
cards.quote: Fasciclin II is a member of the immunoglobulin (Ig) superfamily of adhesion molecules and binds Fasciclin II on a neighbouring axon.

cards.front: In Drosophila, how should loss of Fasciclin II versus extra Fasciclin II on motor axons affect bundling and exit at a branch point?
cards.back: Loss lets axons in certain normally bundled pathways drift apart. Extra Fasciclin II keeps motor axons in the nerve past their exit; adhesion must support travel yet permit release.
cards.quote: Opposite manipulations give opposite results, so the amount of adhesion between axons matters.

cards.front: A second mutation that lessens a defect caused by a first mutation produces genetic {{c1::suppression}}.
cards.back: The original defect becomes less severe.
cards.quote: suppression: a second mutation lessens the defect caused by the first

cards.front: In Drosophila, a beat mutant motor axon stays in its nerve. Partial loss of Fasciclin II suppresses the exit defect. How does this result relate to the bypass caused by extra Fasciclin II?
cards.back: Both support a balance between bundle adhesion and guidance away from it. Lowering adhesion can compensate for losing Beat; raising adhesion can prevent exit even when Beat is present.
cards.quote: So lowering adhesion between axons can compensate for losing Beat, and exit depends on a balance between bundle adhesion and guidance away from the bundle.

cards.front: In Drosophila, does suppression of the beat exit defect by reducing Fasciclin II prove that Beat directly inhibits Fasciclin II? Explain an alternative consistent with the result.
cards.back: No. The balance rule allows reduced adhesion to let remaining guidance inputs drive exit. Suppression therefore supports compensation without establishing a direct molecular interaction or direct anti-adhesive action.
cards.quote: Suppression alone does not distinguish a direct anti-adhesive action of Beat from guidance toward an external pathway, and does not show that Beat acts on Fasciclin II.

cards.front: How did chick motor growth cones at the plexus or muscle-nerve branches differ from those in straight route segments?
cards.back: They were larger, more lamellipodial and followed more convoluted paths; growth cones in straight stretches were small and simple.
cards.quote: At the plexus and where muscle nerves branch off, the growth cones were larger, more lamellipodial and followed more convoluted paths.

cards.front: A researcher uses fixed chick embryos to claim that complex growth cones at a plexus move slowly. What can the observations support, and what additional evidence is needed?
cards.back: They support an association between shape and route location, not a speed measurement. Following growth cones over time would be needed to measure movement or pausing.
cards.quote: These were fixed embryos, so the study saw shape, not speed;

cards.front: Why can the same guidance molecule attract one growth cone and repel another?
cards.back: Its effect depends on the growth cone’s receptors and internal state. Attraction or repulsion describes the response in a particular context, not an invariant molecular property.
cards.quote: A cue is a message, and the receptors and internal state of the growth cone decide what it means.

cards.front: In the simplified netrin-1 receptor comparison, predict the response of a DCC-only growth cone versus one carrying DCC and UNC5, and explain the difference.
cards.back: DCC alone can support attraction; DCC with UNC5 can support repulsion. Changing the receptor combination changes how the same cue is read.
cards.quote: netrin-1 can attract growth cones that carry the receptor DCC alone and repel those that carry DCC with a second receptor, UNC5.

cards.front: Cultured Xenopus spinal growth cones switch from approaching netrin-1 to retreating when cAMP signaling is lowered, without changing the cue. What does this perturbation demonstrate?
cards.back: An internal signaling change can reverse the response to the same external cue; the cue alone does not determine attraction versus repulsion.
cards.quote: In cultured Xenopus spinal neurons, lowering cAMP signaling turned attraction to netrin-1 into repulsion.

cards.front: How can a small set of cue families guide many axon types through several choice points without a unique cue for every connection?
cards.back: The local-reading rule lets each choice point reuse cue families in new combinations. Receptor combinations and internal state alter their meaning, so the same cue can support different choices along different routes.
cards.quote: Cues act in combination, and each choice point reuses the same few families in a new place and a new combination.

cards.front: In the steady-state uniform-tissue model, mean cue lifetime is λ²/D. For λ = 1 mm and D = 10 to 30 µm²/s, estimate the mean lifetime range in hours.
cards.back: Convert λ to 1,000 µm. Lifetime = (1,000 µm)²/D: about 33,333–100,000 s, or about 9–28 h. The larger D gives the shorter lifetime.
cards.quote: so the cue's mean lifetime, 1/k, equals λ²/D.
cards.section: How far can a secreted cue reach?

cards.front: What qualification is needed when describing netrin-1 as a long-range floor-plate attractant in the mouse embryo?
cards.back: Much of its effect comes from locally deposited netrin-1 along the path. Floor-plate netrin, with Sonic hedgehog, may still act at a distance near the midline.
cards.quote: netrin-1 laid down by ventricular-zone progenitors along the path carries much of the effect and acts locally,

cards.front: Why can axon extension on simple charged coatings be fastest at intermediate adhesion?
cards.back: Too little grip lets actin slip backward; too much prevents release of old adhesions. Intermediate adhesion can support both traction and release.
cards.quote: With too little grip, the actin network slips backward and the edge does not advance. With too much, the growth cone cannot let go of old adhesions to move on.

cards.front: In a hypothetical culture, an axon grows for 20 h at 45 µm/h on a moderately adhesive coating. How long would the same distance take at 15 µm/h on a highly adhesive coating?
cards.back: Distance = 45 µm/h × 20 h = 900 µm. Time on the highly adhesive coating = 900 µm ÷ 15 µm/h = 60 h.
cards.quote: how sticky a surface is turned out to be a poor predictor of growth rate.

cards.front: Blocking integrins stops axon extension on laminin, but a second coating keeps cell bodies attached. What role does this separate from simple cell attachment, and why is that control essential?
cards.back: Integrins are needed for extension on laminin beyond simply holding cell bodies down. The control separates soma attachment from extension; without it, detachment could explain lost outgrowth. The clutch rule links productive adhesion to advance.
cards.quote: Outgrowth on laminin stopped while the cells stayed down, so integrins were needed for extension, not only to hold the cell on.

cards.front: Extracellular calcium is removed from a growth-cone contact assay that depends on N-cadherin. What happens to that adhesion, and why?
cards.back: It should weaken because cadherin-mediated binding requires calcium.
cards.quote: Cadherins, such as N-cadherin, which need calcium and bind the same cadherin on another cell.

cards.front: Why can a uniform growth-permissive coating support axon extension without selecting a direction?
cards.back: It offers support everywhere but no directional difference. A border or gradient can provide the asymmetry needed to steer.
cards.quote: A uniform coat of laminin permits growth but gives no direction. A border or a gradient can.

cards.front: Time-lapse observations show branches tending to form at sites where a growth cone paused. Does that association establish that pausing causes branching?
cards.back: No. It establishes a relationship between pausing and branch location, not causation. A perturbation that separates pausing from other influences would be needed to test a causal role.
cards.quote: branches tend to form where a growth cone has stopped to read its surroundings.
